translations.literal: The Odes says, "High is that southern mountain, with its rocks precipitous; illustrious are you, Master Yin, and the people all look to you.
translations.idiomatic: The Classic of Poetry says: "Lofty stands that southern mountain, its crags sheer as a wall; awesome sits Minister Yin, and every eye is fixed on you."

sentences.zh: 」言其德行高峻，動必以禮耳。

translations.literal: "It means that his virtue and conduct are lofty and precipitous, and every movement must be by ritual.
translations.idiomatic: The verse praises a minister whose virtue towers so high that every step follows ritual.

sentences.zh: 丘明有言：「儉，德之恭；

translations.literal: Qiu Ming has a saying, 'Frugality is the honour of virtue;
translations.idiomatic: Zuo Qiuming adds: frugality is the crown of virtue;

sentences.zh: 侈，惡之大也。

translations.literal: extravagance is the greatest of evils.
translations.idiomatic: extravagance is the chief of vices.

sentences.zh: 」大晉受命，勞廉隱約，曾受寵二代，顯赫累世。

translations.literal: Great Jin received the mandate, encouraging the frugal and restraining the extravagant; Zeng received favour through two reigns, manifest and glorious for generations.
translations.idiomatic: When the Great Jin took the throne it honoured modesty; He Zeng basked in favour across two reigns and dazzled for generations.

sentences.zh: 暨乎耳順之年，身兼三公之位，食大國之租，荷保傅之貴，執司徒之均。

translations.literal: Coming to the years past sixty, his person combined the three dukes' posts, ate the rent of a great state, bore the honour of tutor and protector, and held the Minister of Education's balancing staff.
translations.idiomatic: Past his sixtieth year he piled three dukedoms on one frame, drew income from a great princedom, doubled as tutor and guardian, and wielded the minister of education's staff of equity.

sentences.zh: 二子皆金貂卿校，列於帝側。

translations.literal: Both sons wore gold marten insignia as ministers and colonels, arrayed at the emperor's side.
translations.idiomatic: Both sons flanked the throne in gold-marten ministerial rank.

sentences.zh: 方之古人，責深負重，雖舉門盡死，猶不稱位。

translations.literal: Compared to men of antiquity, the burden demanded of him was deep and heavy; though his whole gate died, it would still not match the position.
translations.idiomatic: Set against ancient exemplars, the duty was crushing: had his entire household perished in service it would scarcely match such rank.

sentences.zh: 而乃驕奢過度，名被九域，行不履道，而享位非常。

translations.literal: Yet he was arrogant and extravagant beyond measure; his name covered the nine regions; his conduct did not tread the Way, yet he enjoyed position beyond the norm.
translations.idiomatic: Instead he flaunted luxury to every corner of the realm, walked outside the Way, yet clung to offices no norm would allow.

sentences.zh: 以古義言之，非惟失輔相之宜，違斷金之利也。

translations.literal: Speaking by ancient meaning, not only did he miss the fitness of a minister, he also violated the profit of severing metal.
translations.idiomatic: By classical standards he failed both as minister and as steadfast partner warned of in the Changes.

sentences.zh: 穢皇代之美，壞人倫之教，生天下之醜，示後生之傲，莫大於此。

translations.literal: He defiled the beauty of the august age and ruined the teaching of human relations; nothing greater than this for producing ugliness in the world and displaying arrogance to later born.
translations.idiomatic: Nothing did more to stain the new dynasty's brilliance, corrupt public ethics, advertise vice to the world, and teach the young to sneer at restraint.

sentences.zh: 自近世以來，宰臣輔相，未有受垢辱之聲，被有司之劾，父子塵累而蒙恩貸若曾者也。

translations.literal: From recent generations onward, chief ministers and assisting ministers have not borne a reputation of filth and insult, nor been impeached by the authorities, with father and son dust-laden yet receiving grace and pardon as Zeng did.
translations.idiomatic: In living memory no chief minister has wallowed in scandal, faced censorial impeachment, dragged his sons through the mire, and still won lavish pardon as He Zeng did.

sentences.zh: 周公吊二季之陵遲，哀大教之不行，於是作諡以紀其終。

translations.literal: The Duke of Zhou mourned the decline of the two Jis and pitied that the great teaching did not proceed; therefore he made posthumous names to record their ends.
translations.idiomatic: The Duke of Zhou lamented how the Ji brothers had slipped from virtue and how the great teaching faltered, which is why posthumous names were invented—to seal a life's moral ledger.

sentences.zh: 曾參奉之，啟手歸全，易簀而沒，蓋明慎終，死而後已。

translations.literal: Zeng Shen upheld it, spreading his hands to return whole, changed the mat and died—thus clarifying careful attention to the end, dying only when finished.
translations.idiomatic: Zeng Shen followed that lesson, straightening his limbs on his deathbed and refusing an improper mat—proof that a gentleman polishes his end to the last breath.

sentences.zh: 齊之史氏，亂世陪臣耳，猶書君賊，累死不懲。

translations.literal: The historiographers of Qi were only disorderly retainers, yet they still wrote that the ruler was a traitor, and piled up deaths without correcting.
translations.idiomatic: Even Qi scribes, mere retainers in a chaotic age, branded a murderous lord and kept recording despite repeated peril.

sentences.zh: 況於皇代守典之官，敢畏強盛，而不盡禮。

translations.literal: How much more must officials of the august age who guard the canons dare to fear the powerful and not exhaust ritual!
translations.idiomatic: How much less may officers of our dynasty, charged with preserving the rites, flinch from the mighty and shrink from speaking the full ritual truth!

sentences.zh: 管子有言：「禮義廉恥，是謂四維，四維不張，國乃滅亡。

translations.literal: Guanzi has a saying, 'Propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame are called the four cords; if the four cords are not stretched, the state will perish.
translations.idiomatic: Guan Zhong said propriety, justice, integrity, and honour are the four cables of state; let them slack and the realm collapses.

sentences.zh: 」宰相大臣，人之表儀，若生極其情，死又無貶，是則帝室無正刑也。

translations.literal: Ministers and grandees are people's models; if in life they indulge their passions and in death receive no demotion, then the imperial house has no correct punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Chief ministers are the realm's mirror: if they live in open excess yet escape posthumous censure, the court has no standard of justice left.

sentences.zh: 王公貴人，復何畏哉！

translations.literal: What then do the noble princes and honoured men still fear!
translations.idiomatic: Why should great lords fear the law at all?

sentences.zh: 所謂四維，復何寄乎！

translations.literal: The so-called four cords—on what are they to rely!
translations.idiomatic: And where are those four moral cables supposed to anchor themselves?

sentences.zh: 謹按《諡法》：「名與實爽曰繆，怙亂肆行曰醜。

translations.literal: Respectfully examining the Posthumous Canon: 'When name and reality diverge, it is called Miu; when relying on disorder one acts recklessly, it is called Chou.
translations.idiomatic: The Posthumous Canon states: when title and deed diverge the name is Miu; when a man rides chaos to do as he pleases the name is Chou.

sentences.zh: 」曾之行己，皆與此同，宜諡繆醜公。

translations.literal: Zeng's conduct in all respects matches this; he should be posthumously titled Duke Miu-Chou.
translations.idiomatic: He Zeng's life fits both clauses; he should be called Duke Miu-Chou.

sentences.zh: 時雖不同秀議，而聞者懼焉。

translations.literal: At the time, though they did not agree with Xiu's deliberation, those who heard were fearful.
translations.idiomatic: The court rejected Qin Xiu's formula, yet everyone who heard it shivered.

sentences.zh: 秀性忌讒佞，疾之如仇，素輕鄙賈充，及伐吳之役，聞其為大都督，謂所親者曰：「充文案小才，乃居伐國大任，吾將哭以送師。

translations.literal: Xiu by nature hated slanderers and treated them like enemies; he always despised Jia Chong, and when the campaign to attack Wu arose, hearing that Chong was Grand Commander, he said to those close to him, "Chong is a petty talent for paperwork, yet occupies the great charge of attacking a state; I will weep to send off the army.
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu detested flatterers as mortal foes and scorned Jia Chong. When the Wu campaign began and Jia Chong was named grand commander, Qin told friends, "A clerk's wit now commands a conquest—I mean to weep the hosts onto the road."

sentences.zh: 」或止秀曰：「昔蹇叔知秦軍必敗，故哭送其子耳。

translations.literal: Someone stopped Xiu, saying, "In olden times Jian Shu knew the Qin army would be defeated, therefore he wept to send off his son.
translations.idiomatic: A friend warned him: "Jian Shu wept only because he foresaw Qin's defeat.

sentences.zh: 今吳君無道，國有自亡之形，群率踐境，將不戰而潰。

translations.literal: Now the lord of Wu is without the Way; his state has the form of destroying itself; hosts tread his borders and will collapse without battle.
translations.idiomatic: Wu is ruled by a tyrant ripe for collapse; our armies will walk in unopposed.

sentences.zh: 子之哭也，既為不智，乃不赦之罪。

translations.literal: Your weeping would be both unwise and an unpardonable crime.
translations.idiomatic: To wail now would be folly and a punishable insult.

sentences.zh: 」於是乃止。

translations.literal: Thereupon he stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu relented.

sentences.zh: 及孫皓降于王濬，充未之知，方以吳未可平，抗表請班師。

translations.literal: When Sun Hao surrendered to Wang Jun, Chong did not yet know it, and was still thinking Wu could not be pacified, resisting with a memorial requesting withdrawal of the army.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao had already capitulated to Wang Jun before Jia Chong heard the news; he was still insisting Wu could not be taken and begging to recall the troops.

sentences.zh: 充表與告捷同至，朝野以充位居人上，智出人下，僉以秀為知言。

translations.literal: Chong's memorial arrived together with the victory report; court and countryside, because Chong occupied a position above others yet wisdom was below others, all considered Xiu to have spoken with knowledge.
translations.idiomatic: Jia Chong's plea reached court the same day as the victory bulletin, and the whole capital concluded that a man so high in rank and so low in judgment proved Qin Xiu a prophet.

sentences.zh: 及充薨，秀議曰：「充舍宗族弗授，而以異姓為後，悖禮溺情，以亂大倫。

translations.literal: When Chong died, Xiu deliberated, saying, "Chong rejected his agnates and would not appoint them heir, yet took a different surname as successor—violating ritual and drowning feeling, thereby disordering the great human bonds.
translations.idiomatic: After Jia Chong died Qin Xiu argued that he had spurned his own kin for heirs and adopted an outsider—trampling ritual and sentiment alike to wreck the natural order of the family.

sentences.zh: 昔鄫養外孫莒公子為後，《春秋》書'莒人滅鄫'。

translations.literal: In olden times Zeng raised his maternal grandson, the heir of Ju's lord, as successor; the Spring and Autumn Annals records 'the people of Ju destroyed Zeng.'
translations.idiomatic: When the state of Zeng made a Ju prince's grandson heir, the Annals recorded it as "Ju extinguished Zeng".

sentences.zh: 聖人豈不知外孫親邪！

translations.literal: Did the sage not know a grandson by a daughter is close!
translations.idiomatic: The sage knew full well how dear a daughter's son can be;

sentences.zh: 但以義推之，則無父子耳。

translations.literal: But when pushed by righteousness, there is no father-son relation.
translations.idiomatic: duty still forbids treating him as a true heir.

sentences.zh: 又案詔書'自非功如太宰，始封無後如太宰，所取必己自出如太宰，不得以為比'。

translations.literal: Moreover, examining the edict's words, 'Unless merit matches the Grand Tutor, unless the first enfeoffment has no heir as with the Grand Tutor, unless what is taken must be from oneself as with the Grand Tutor, it cannot be taken as precedent.
translations.idiomatic: The throne's own edict said no precedent applies unless the merit, the lack of heirs, and the blood tie all match the Grand Tutor's unique case.

sentences.zh: 然則以外孫為後，自非元功顯德，不之得也。

translations.literal: Thus to take a maternal grandson as heir is, unless for primordial merit and manifest virtue, not to be obtained.
translations.idiomatic: Adopting a daughter's son is therefore barred except for founders of towering merit.

sentences.zh: 天子之禮，蓋可然乎？

translations.literal: Can the Son of Heaven's ritual be thus!
translations.idiomatic: May the Son of Heaven's rites be bent that far?

sentences.zh: 絕父祖之血食，開朝廷之禍門。

translations.literal: It cuts off the blood offerings of father and grandfather and opens a gate of disaster for the court.
translations.idiomatic: It severs ancestral sacrifice at the root and invites catastrophe into the court.

sentences.zh: 《諡法》'昏亂紀度曰荒'，請諡荒公。

translations.literal: The Posthumous Canon says, 'Confusing and disordering the norms is called Huang'; I request the posthumous name Duke Huang.
translations.idiomatic: The Posthumous Canon calls a man who scrambles the norms "Huang"; Jia Chong should be Duke Huang.

sentences.zh: 」不從。

translations.literal: They did not follow.
translations.idiomatic: The court refused.

sentences.zh: 王濬有平吳之勳，而為王渾所譖毀。

translations.literal: Wang Jun had the merit of pacifying Wu, yet was slandered and ruined by Wang Hun.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jun earned the credit for conquering Wu but Wang Hun's slander nearly ruined him.

sentences.zh: 帝雖不從，無明賞罰，以濬為輔國大將軍，天下咸為之怨。

translations.literal: Though the Emperor did not follow, there was no clear reward or punishment, and he made Jun General Who Supports the State; all under Heaven resented it on his behalf.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor declined Qin Xiu's advice yet never settled the score fairly, merely naming Wang Jun general who supports the state—an insult the realm resented on his behalf.

sentences.zh: 秀乃上言曰：「自大晉啟祚，輔國之號，率以舊恩。

translations.literal: Thereupon Xiu submitted a statement, saying, "Since Great Jin opened its mandate, the title General Who Supports the State has always gone to old favour.
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu therefore wrote: "Since our dynasty began, the title general who supports the state has been a sinecure for court favourites.

sentences.zh: 此為王濬無功之時，受九列之顯位，立功之後更得寵人之辱號也。

translations.literal: This means that Wang Jun, at the time he had no merit, received the eminent rank of the nine columns, and after establishing merit then again received the humiliating title of a favoured person.
translations.idiomatic: So Wang Jun first drew a minister's stipend without merit, then earned the sneering reward reserved for imperial pets.

sentences.zh: 四海視之，孰不失望！

translations.literal: All within the Four Seas look on it—who would not be disappointed!
translations.idiomatic: Everyone under heaven sees the slight—who could fail to feel cheated?

sentences.zh: 蜀小吳大，平蜀之後，二將皆就加三事，今濬還而降等，天下安得不惑乎！

translations.literal: Shu is small and Wu is large; after pacifying Shu, both generals were thereupon advanced to the three offices; now Jun returns and is lowered in rank—how can All-under-Heaven not be perplexed!
translations.idiomatic: Shu was the lesser foe, Wu the greater: after Shu fell both generals who took it were raised to the three highest posts. Wang Jun conquers Wu yet is demoted—how can the realm not be baffled?

sentences.zh: 吳之未亡也，雖以三祖之神武，猶躬受其屈。

translations.literal: Before Wu's destruction, though with the divine martialness of the three ancestors, they still personally received its humiliation.
translations.idiomatic: Even the three martial founders had to swallow indignities from Wu while it still stood.

sentences.zh: 以孫皓之虛名，足以驚動諸夏，每一小出，雖聖心知其垂亡，然中國輒懷惶怖。

translations.literal: With Sun Hao's empty name, it was enough to startle the central states; each time he made a small sally, though the sage heart knew he was on the verge of perishing, yet the central lands always harboured fear and terror.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao's hollow prestige still shook the heartland: each time he sortied, the court knew he was dying, yet every garrison trembled as if doom were near.

sentences.zh: 當爾時，有能借天子百萬之眾，平而有之，與國家結兄弟之交，臣恐朝野實皆甘之耳。

translations.literal: At such a time, had there been one who could borrow a million hosts of the Son of Heaven, pacify and possess it, and with the state knot brotherhood—your servant fears court and countryside would in truth all be willing.
translations.idiomatic: Had someone offered to borrow the emperor's hosts, crush Wu, and seal a brotherly pact with the throne, I suspect every minister would have leapt at the bargain.

sentences.zh: 今濬舉蜀、漢之卒，數旬而平吳，雖舉吳人之財寶以與之，本非己分有焉，而遽與計校乎？」

translations.literal: Now Jun raised the troops of Shu and Han and in several tens of days pacified Wu; though one gathered the Wu people's treasures and gave them to him, fundamentally it was not what he himself had a share in—yet hastily to haggle over reckoning with him?
translations.idiomatic: Wang Jun led the armies of the west and finished Wu in weeks. Even if you poured Wu's plunder into his lap, it would still be largesse he never owned—yet you quibble over his reward?

sentences.zh: 後與劉暾等同議齊王攸事，忤旨，除名。

translations.literal: Later, together with Liu Tun and others he deliberated on the affair of Prince Sima You of Qi, contravening the intent, and was removed from name.
translations.idiomatic: Later he joined Liu Tun and others debating Prince Sima You's fief issue, crossed the emperor's will, and was stricken from the rolls.

sentences.zh: 尋復起為博士。

translations.literal: Before long he was again raised as erudit.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled to a doctorate.

sentences.zh: 秀性悻直，與物多忤。

translations.literal: Xiu's nature was resentful and straight; with things he often clashed.
translations.idiomatic: Qin Xiu was prickly and blunt, and crossed paths with many.

sentences.zh: 為博士前後垂二十年，卒於官。

translations.literal: As erudit before and after nearly twenty years, he died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He spent the better part of two decades as a doctoral scholar and died in harness.

sentences.zh: 【史評】

translations.literal: 【Historiographer's Appraisal】
translations.idiomatic: Historiographer's appraisal

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：齊獻王以明德茂親，經邦論道，允厘庶績，式敘彝倫。

translations.literal: The court historians say: Prince Xian of Qi, by enlightened virtue and flourishing kinship, ordered the state and discussed the Way, truly regulated the myriad tasks and thereby set in order the constant human bonds.
translations.idiomatic: The historians write: Prince Xian of Qi combined royal virtue with true kinship—he was meant to steady the realm, guide policy, align every branch of government, and model the human order.

sentences.zh: 武帝納奸諂之邪謀，懷紹終之遠慮，遂乃君茲青土，作牧東籓。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu adopted treacherous and sycophantic evil counsel, harboured distant thoughts about succession's end, and therefore lorded him over this green soil, making him shepherd the eastern fief.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu listened to corrupt advisers, brooded on long-term succession, and so banished him to a distant green fief to rule the eastern march.

sentences.zh: 遠邇驚嗟，朝野失望。

translations.literal: Far and near were startled and sighed; court and countryside were disappointed.
translations.idiomatic: The news drew gasps near and far; court and countryside alike felt betrayed.

sentences.zh: 曹志等服膺教義，方軌儒門，蹇蹇匪躬，慺慺體國。

translations.literal: Therefore Cao Zhi and others embraced the teaching's meaning, aligned their tracks with the Confucian gate, were steadfast though not for themselves alone, and earnestly embodied the state.
translations.idiomatic: Men like Cao Zhi took the rites to heart, kept to the Confucian path, risked themselves without self-interest, and wore the state's worries on their sleeves.

sentences.zh: 故能抗言鳳闕，忤犯龍鱗，身雖暫屈，道亦弘矣！

translations.literal: Therefore they could speak boldly at the phoenix tower, offend the dragon scales; though their persons for a time were bent, the Way was thereby enlarged!
translations.idiomatic: So they could speak truth at the palace gate and brush the emperor's temper: though their careers bent for a season, the Way itself grew stronger.

sentences.zh: 庾氏世載清德，見稱於世，汝潁之多奇士，斯焉取斯。

translations.literal: The Yu clan for generations bore pure virtue and was praised in the age; among the many strange scholars of Ru and Ying, this is what was taken from them.
translations.idiomatic: For generations the Yu family stood for unstained honour in Ru and Ying, a house from which the age drew its finest scholars.

sentences.zh: 謀甫素疾佞邪，而發因醉飽，投鼠忌器，豈易由言。

translations.literal: Moufu by nature hated flattery and evil, yet his outburst came from wine and satiety; to strike at a rat yet fear the vessel—is it easy to speak thereby.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Chun loathed sycophants by nature, yet wine loosened his tongue; striking the rat without smashing the vase is never simple.

sentences.zh: 竊人之財，猶謂之盜，子玄假譽攘善，將非盜乎！

translations.literal: To steal people's goods is still called theft; Zixuan borrowed fame and plundered excellence—is he not a thief!
translations.idiomatic: Theft of another's goods is theft by law; Guo Zixuan stole another's glory—what is that if not theft?

sentences.zh: 贊曰：魏氏維城，濟北知名。

translations.literal: The encomium says: Of Wei's bulwarks, Jibei's name was known.
translations.idiomatic: The verse praises: Among Wei's princely shields, Jibei's name shone bright.

sentences.zh: 潁川多士，峻亦飛英。

translations.literal: Yingchuan had many gentlemen, and Jun too flew in splendour.
translations.idiomatic: Yingchuan bred statesmen, and Yu Jun rose among them.

sentences.zh: 長岑徇義，祭酒遺榮。

translations.literal: Changcen followed righteousness; the Libationer cast away glory.
translations.idiomatic: The lord of Changcen chose duty; the libationer turned his back on pomp.

sentences.zh: 謀甫三爵，酗醟斯作。

translations.literal: Moufu at three cups, drunken riot then arose.
translations.idiomatic: Three cups undid Yu Moufu, and drunken brawling followed.

sentences.zh: 象既攘善，秀惟癉惡。

translations.literal: Xiang having plundered excellence, Xiu alone exposed evil.
translations.idiomatic: Guo Xiang stole the credit; Qin Xiu exposed the wicked.

sentences.zh: 旉獻嘉謀，幾趨鼎鑊。

translations.literal: Fu presented fine counsel and nearly marched to the cauldron's boil.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Fu offered wise remonstrance and nearly boiled in the cauldron for it.
